warmup.q: A Kotlin service has val rates by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { loadRates() }. Eight request threads read rates for the first time at the same moment. How many times can loadRates() run?
options: Exactly once, because lazy always takes a lock
Up to eight times, but every thread ends up with the same value
Up to eight times, and each thread may keep its own value
Zero times until the main thread reads it first
warmup.why: PUBLICATION takes no lock. Every thread that finds the value missing runs the initializer, and the first result stored wins; the rest are thrown away. So loadRates() can run eight times while all callers see one value. The default mode, SYNCHRONIZED, is the one that runs it once. Threads keeping their own values is what NONE allows.

sections.h: A pattern is a name for a design you keep meeting
sections.html:
A design pattern is a name for a design that keeps showing up: the problem, the shape of the solution, and what it costs you. It is a word in a shared vocabulary. It is not a class template to paste.

The 1994 "Gang of Four" book listed 23 patterns, written for C++ and Smalltalk. Java at the time had no lambdas, no records and no sealed types, and many of those patterns were workarounds for exactly that. The names are still worth knowing. In a code review, "put a decorator around the issuer client" is a whole design in a few words. And you need the names to recognise a pattern when a language feature or a framework hands it to you under another name.

In Java 21+ and Kotlin 2.x, the 23 sort into three groups. This track follows them.

  • The language absorbed them. Strategy, Command and Template Method become function values. State and Visitor become a sealed type plus an exhaustive switch or when. Builder mostly becomes Kotlin's named and default arguments. Singleton becomes an enum or a Kotlin object. Decorator becomes Kotlin's by delegation.
  • A framework absorbed them. Proxy lives inside Spring and Quarkus. Chain of Responsibility is a servlet filter chain or an HTTP client interceptor. Observer is Kotlin Flow, Reactor and java.util.concurrent.Flow.
  • You still design them by hand. Adapter, Facade, Bridge, Composite, Mediator and Flyweight are about how you cut up your own domain, and no feature does that for you.

The intent of an absorbed pattern survives. Strategy still means "swap the algorithm without touching the caller". What changed is the price. A strategy used to be an interface and three classes. Now it is a lambda in a map, so you use it ten times more often and stop calling it a pattern.

Brian Goetz, Java's language architect, gave the strongest version of this in a 2018 design note on pattern matching: with powerful enough pattern matching, "the Visitor pattern is almost completely unnecessary". The same note says this does not make inheritance and virtual methods wrong. That is the position of this track too. Learn the intent, then reach for the cheapest feature that delivers it, and know when the feature is not enough.

try.title: Find five patterns in the JDK
steps: Read main in PatternsYouAlreadyUse below (Java or Kotlin, they print the same). Write down what each of the six lines will print before you run anything.
Run it from labs/ with the command below.
Name the pattern behind each line: singleton, flyweight, read-through view (proxy) or strategy. Which line surprised you?

code.title: PatternsYouAlreadyUse.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.Currency; import java.util.List; import java.util.Collections; /** Five patterns hiding in the JDK. Predict each line before you run it. */ public class PatternsYouAlreadyUse { record Payment(String id, long amountMinor) {} public static void main(String[] args) { // Singleton: one Runtime per JVM, no public constructor System.out.println("1. Runtime is a singleton: " + (Runtime.getRuntime() == Runtime.getRuntime())); // Flyweight: Integer.valueOf caches -128..127, Currency keeps one instance per code Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println("2. 127 == 127 (boxed): " + (a == b)); System.out.println("3. 128 == 128 (boxed): " + (c == d)); System.out.println("4. EUR == EUR (Currency): " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") == Currency.getInstance("EUR"))); // Proxy/decorator view: unmodifiableList reads through to the list it wraps List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("p-1")); List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(ids); ids.add("p-2"); System.out.println("5. view after ids.add(\"p-2\"): " + view); // Strategy: a Comparator is an algorithm you pass in, and a lambda is enough to make one List<Payment> payments = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Payment("p-9", 500), new Payment("p-3", 12_000))); payments.sort(Comparator.comparing(Payment::amountMinor).reversed()); System.out.println("6. sorted by amount, desc: " + payments.stream().map(Payment::id).toList()); } }

alt.title: PatternsYouAlreadyUse.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.Collections import java.util.Currency // Five patterns hiding in the JDK and the Kotlin standard library. Predict each line before you run it. private data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long) fun main() { // Singleton: one Runtime per JVM, no public constructor println("1. Runtime is a singleton: " + (Runtime.getRuntime() === Runtime.getRuntime())) // Flyweight: a nullable Int is a boxed java.lang.Integer, and Integer.valueOf caches -128..127 val a: Int? = 127; val b: Int? = 127; val c: Int? = 128; val d: Int? = 128 println("2. 127 === 127 (boxed): " + (a as Any === b as Any)) println("3. 128 === 128 (boxed): " + (c as Any === d as Any)) println("4. EUR === EUR (Currency): " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") === Currency.getInstance("EUR"))) // Proxy/decorator view: unmodifiableList reads through to the list it wraps val ids = mutableListOf("p-1") val view: List<String> = Collections.unmodifiableList(ids) ids += "p-2" println("5. view after ids += \"p-2\": $view") // Strategy: a Comparator is an algorithm you pass in; compareByDescending builds one from a lambda val payments = listOf(Payment("p-9", 500), Payment("p-3", 12_000)) println("6. sorted by amount, desc: " + payments.sortedWith(compareByDescending { it.amountMinor }).map { it.id }) }

try.expect: It prints true, true, false, true, [p-1, p-2] and [p-3, p-9]. Line 3 surprises most people: Integer.valueOf only caches -128 to 127, so two boxed 128s are different objects. Line 5 shows that unmodifiableList is a view that reads through to the list it wraps. It blocks writes through the view, and it is not a copy.

sections.h: Singleton in Java: enum, holder and double-checked locking
sections.html:
A singleton is a class with exactly one instance and one place to get it. The JDK has its own: the Runtime Javadoc says every Java application has a single instance of Runtime, and an application cannot create its own.

The "one" is easy. The hard part is "one, created lazily, by many threads at once". The naive version is the check-then-act race from Race conditions: why count++ lies:

Java
static FxRates instance;
static FxRates getInstance() {
    if (instance == null) instance = new FxRates();   // two threads can both see null
    return instance;
}
Kotlin
private var instance: FxRates? = null
fun fxRates(): FxRates {
    if (instance == null) instance = FxRates()        // the same race in Kotlin
    return instance!!
}

If loading FxRates takes 20 ms and eight request threads arrive together, all eight see null and you build eight. Here are the correct versions, in the order I reach for them.

Java
enum IdGenerator {                      // 1. enum: the JVM makes exactly one INSTANCE
    INSTANCE;
    private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong();
    long nextId() { return next.incrementAndGet(); }
}

final class FxRates {                   // 2. holder: lazy, no lock on the fast path
    private FxRates() { }
    private static final class Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); }
    static FxRates getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}
Kotlin
enum class IdGenerator {                // 1. enum works the same in Kotlin
    INSTANCE;
    private val next = AtomicLong()
    fun nextId() = next.incrementAndGet()
}

class FxRates private constructor() {   // 2. holder: a private object nested in the companion
    companion object {
        private object Holder { val INSTANCE = FxRates() }
        fun getInstance(): FxRates = Holder.INSTANCE
    }
}

The enum is what Effective Java (item 3) calls the preferred approach. Serialization and reflection can't make a second instance, and you write no locking code. Use it when the object is cheap or needed at startup anyway.

The holder idiom is for an expensive object you want lazily. The JVM initializes the nested Holder class the first time anyone reads Holder.INSTANCE. Class initialization runs once, under a lock the JVM owns, so every later call is a plain static read.

The third tool is double-checked locking (DCL), from Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders in the memory model track. The holder only works for static fields. When the lazy value lives in an instance field, such as one cache per merchant or a registry your DI container creates, DCL is the answer:

Java
private volatile Map<String, String> table;
Map<String, String> table() {
    Map<String, String> t = table;       // one volatile read on the fast path
    if (t == null) {
        synchronized (lock) {
            t = table;                   // re-check: another thread may have won
            if (t == null) table = t = load();
        }
    }
    return t;
}
Kotlin
@Volatile private var table: Map<String, String>? = null
fun table(): Map<String, String> {
    table?.let { return it }             // one volatile read on the fast path
    synchronized(lock) {
        table?.let { return it }         // re-check: another thread may have won
        return load().also { table = it }
    }
}

Leave out volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin) and another thread can see a non-null reference to a map whose contents it can't see yet. That is the lab for this lesson.

try.title: Build eight singletons by accident
steps: Predict: when eight threads call the racy getInstance together, how many FxRates get built? And with the holder?
Delete the Thread.sleep(20) line in the constructor (FxRates in Java, SlowRates in Kotlin) and run it three more times. Did the race go away?

code.title: LazyRaceDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Eight threads ask for a "singleton" at the same moment. How many get built? */ public class LazyRaceDemo { static final AtomicInteger built = new AtomicInteger(); static final class FxRates { FxRates() { built.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // a slow load } } // broken: check-then-act on a plain static field static FxRates racy; static FxRates racyGet() { if (racy == null) racy = new FxRates(); return racy; } // initialization-on-demand holder: the JVM runs Holder's static init once, under its class-init lock static final class Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); } static FxRates holderGet() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { report("racy check-then-act", LazyRaceDemo::racyGet); report("holder idiom ", LazyRaceDemo::holderGet); } static void report(String name, Supplier<FxRates> get) throws InterruptedException { built.set(0); Set<Object> seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(get.get()); }); ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("%s: constructor ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)%n", name, built.get(), seen.size()); } }

alt.title: LazyRaceDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.Collections import java.util.IdentityHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads ask for a "singleton" at the same moment. How many get built? private val built = AtomicInteger() private class SlowRates { init { built.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // a slow load } } // broken: check-then-act on a plain top-level var private var racy: SlowRates? = null private fun racyGet(): SlowRates { if (racy == null) racy = SlowRates() return racy!! } // an object declaration: the JVM runs its static initializer once, under the class-init lock private object RatesHolder { val instance = SlowRates() } private fun holderGet(): SlowRates = RatesHolder.instance private fun report(name: String, get: () -> SlowRates) { built.set(0) val seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); seen += get() } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("$name: constructor ran ${built.get()} time(s), callers saw ${seen.size} instance(s)") } fun main() { report("racy check-then-act", ::racyGet) report("object holder ", ::holderGet) }

try.expect: With the slow constructor, the racy version builds 8 instances and callers see 8 different objects. The holder (an object in the Kotlin twin) builds 1. Without the sleep, the racy count drops to 1, 3 or 4 and changes between runs. The race is still there; the window got smaller. A real config load is slow, which is why this shows up in production and not in your unit test.

sections.h: Kotlin: object and lazy do the locking for you
sections.html:
Kotlin builds the singleton into the language. An object declaration defines a class and its one instance in a single step:

Java
// what the Kotlin compiler writes for that object, give or take
public final class IdGenerator {
    public static final IdGenerator INSTANCE = new IdGenerator();
    private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong();
    private IdGenerator() { }
    public long nextId() { return next.incrementAndGet(); }
}
Kotlin
object IdGenerator {
    private val next = AtomicLong()
    fun nextId() = next.incrementAndGet()
}

The Kotlin docs say the initialization of an object declaration is thread-safe and done on first access. Under the hood the compiler writes a class with a static INSTANCE field, set in its static initializer, as the Java twin shows. That is the same JVM mechanism as the holder idiom.

Two details trip people up. A companion object is initialized when its outer class is loaded, like a Java static initializer. And companion members are not static. They are instance members of the companion object, so Java callers write Money.Companion.of(100) unless you mark the function @JvmStatic.

For a lazy value inside a class, use by lazy. It has three modes, and they behave very differently:

Mode What it does Use it for
SYNCHRONIZED (default) takes a lock; the initializer runs once anything with side effects
PUBLICATION no lock; racing threads may each run the initializer, the first stored value wins cheap, pure computations
NONE no lock and no guarantee across threads values one thread owns

PUBLICATION is the trap. If the initializer opens a connection pool or starts a Kafka consumer, eight concurrent first reads can open eight pools. Seven are thrown away, and nobody closes them.

The default lazy is DCL written once, correctly, in the standard library. It also retries: if the initializer throws, the next access runs it again. In Kotlin, never write DCL by hand.

try.title: Count the lazy initializer runs
steps: Read LazyModes.kt. The Java twin writes each mode by hand, which shows what the modes really do. Predict both lines of output: how many initializer runs, and how many distinct instances, for each mode?
Run it with the command below.
Add trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) at the end of main (in Java: trial("NONE", UnsafeLazy::new);) and run it again. Predict first.

code.title: LazyModes.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads touch a lazy property for the first time, together. Count the initializer runs. class FxService(mode: LazyThreadSafetyMode, private val runs: AtomicInteger) { val rates: Map<String, Double> by lazy(mode) { runs.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // pretend to load rates from a slow service mapOf("EUR/USD" to 1.08) } } fun trial(mode: LazyThreadSafetyMode) { val runs = AtomicInteger() val service = FxService(mode, runs) val seen = java.util.Collections.synchronizedSet(java.util.Collections.newSetFromMap(java.util.IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); seen += service.rates } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)".format(mode, runs.get(), seen.size)) } fun main() { trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED) trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) }

alt.title: LazyModesJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** * Java has no `by lazy`, so here are the three Kotlin modes written by hand. * Eight threads read the value for the first time, together. Count the initializer runs. */ public class LazyModesJava { interface Lazy<T> { T get(); } // SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking; the initializer runs once static final class SynchronizedLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private volatile T value; SynchronizedLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { T v = value; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = value; if (v == null) value = v = init.get(); } } return v; } } // PUBLICATION: no lock; every racer computes, compareAndSet keeps the first stored value static final class PublicationLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private final AtomicReference<T> value = new AtomicReference<>(); PublicationLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { T v = value.get(); if (v != null) return v; value.compareAndSet(null, init.get()); return value.get(); } } // NONE: a plain field, no guarantees across threads static final class UnsafeLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private T value; UnsafeLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { if (value == null) value = init.get(); return value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { trial("SYNCHRONIZED", SynchronizedLazy::new); trial("PUBLICATION", PublicationLazy::new); } static void trial(String mode, java.util.function.Function<Supplier<Map<String, Double>>, Lazy<Map<String, Double>>> make) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Lazy<Map<String, Double>> rates = make.apply(() -> { runs.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return Map.of("EUR/USD", 1.08); }); Set<Object> seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(rates.get()); }); ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)%n", mode, runs.get(), seen.size()); } }

try.expect: SYNCHRONIZED runs the initializer once and callers see 1 instance. PUBLICATION runs it 8 times, yet callers still see 1 instance, because only the first stored value is kept. NONE runs it 8 times and callers see 8 instances: each thread kept the map it built. No warning, no exception.

sections.h: Inject the instance instead of fetching it
sections.html:
Most singletons in a backend service should not be hand-rolled at all. Here is why, in one test you can't write:

Java
class PaymentPricer {
    long priceMinor(Payment p) {
        double rate = FxRates.getInstance().rate(p.currency(), "EUR");   // hidden, global
        return Math.round(p.amountMinor() * rate);
    }
}
Kotlin
class PaymentPricer {
    fun priceMinor(p: Payment): Long {
        val rate = FxRates.rate(p.currency, "EUR")          // FxRates is an object: hidden, global
        return (p.amountMinor * rate).roundToLong()
    }
}

To test priceMinor with a fixed rate of 1.10 you need to control FxRates, and you can't. The instance is global, built once per JVM, and loads real rates. A test that changes its state leaks into the next test, so the suite passes or fails depending on order. Nothing in the constructor of PaymentPricer even tells a reader that it calls an FX service.

Pass the dependency in, typed as an interface:

Java
interface FxRates { double rate(String from, String to); }

class PaymentPricer {
    private final FxRates rates;
    PaymentPricer(FxRates rates) { this.rates = rates; }
    long priceMinor(Payment p) { return Math.round(p.amountMinor() * rates.rate(p.currency(), "EUR")); }
}
// in a test: new PaymentPricer((from, to) -> 1.10)
Kotlin
fun interface FxRates { fun rate(from: String, to: String): Double }

class PaymentPricer(private val rates: FxRates) {
    fun priceMinor(p: Payment): Long = (p.amountMinor * rates.rate(p.currency, "EUR")).roundToLong()
}
// in a test: PaymentPricer { _, _ -> 1.10 }

Production still wants exactly one FxRates. Let the container make it. In Quarkus, an @ApplicationScoped bean is created once per application, on first use. In Spring, singleton is the default scope. You get one instance, lazy creation and shutdown hooks, and the class stays a plain class that a test can construct with new.

A hand-written singleton still fits in a few places: stateless objects such as a comparator or a data object state in a sealed hierarchy, library code that can't assume a container, and state the JVM itself owns, like Runtime. Anything with I/O or configuration gets injected.

The lab's CardNetworkRegistry follows that rule. It is not a static singleton. Its loader comes in through the constructor, so the tests can pass a slow fake loader and count its calls. A container would make one per application, and DCL inside keeps the lazy load safe when eight threads ask at once.

refs.title: Contexts and dependency injection (Quarkus CDI reference)

analogy: A singleton is like the one cash vault in a bank branch. Everyone who needs cash goes to the same vault, and the manager makes sure nobody builds a second one. Lazy initialization is opening the vault only when the first customer asks. Double-checked locking is the manager glancing at the vault door from across the room, and only if it looks shut, walking over with the key and checking again, in case a colleague opened it in the meantime. The analogy breaks on testing: a bank can build a practice vault for training new staff, but a hard-coded getInstance() gives your tests no practice vault at all. That is why you inject it.
world: In a Quarkus payment service you rarely need getInstance(). The card-network config, the FX rate cache and the Kafka producer are @ApplicationScoped beans, so ArC makes one of each and injects them. Hand-written lazy state hides in smaller places: a per-merchant cache that loads fee schedules from Oracle on first use, a lazily built ObjectMapper in a shared library, a Temporal activity implementation that creates its issuer client the first time it runs. Each of those is a check-then-act waiting for two Kafka partitions to hit it in the same millisecond. Use the holder for statics, DCL or Kotlin lazy for instance fields, and keep the loader injectable so a test can count how many times it ran.
mistake: The common mistake is lazy initialization through a plain field: if (cache == null) cache = load();. It passes every single-threaded test, so it looks harmless. Under load, two threads see null, both run load(), and if load() opens connections or registers listeners, one copy leaks. People write it because the race never shows in tests and the fix looks like over-engineering. The fix is one of three idioms: the holder class for a static, double-checked locking with a volatile field for an instance field, or Kotlin by lazy in its default SYNCHRONIZED mode.

compare.title: One instance, and one lazy field, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: FeeSchedules.java
java.html: // singleton: the JVM's class-init lock does the work enum IdGenerator { INSTANCE; private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(); long nextId() { return next.incrementAndGet(); } } // lazy instance field: double-checked locking final class FeeSchedules { private final Supplier<Map<String, Long>> loader; private final Object lock = new Object(); private volatile Map<String, Long> fees; FeeSchedules(Supplier<Map<String, Long>> loader) { this.loader = loader; } Map<String, Long> fees() { Map<String, Long> f = fees; if (f == null) { synchronized (lock) { f = fees; if (f == null) fees = f = Map.copyOf(loader.get()); } } return f; } }

kotlin.title: FeeSchedules.kt
kotlin.html: // singleton: the language makes it object IdGenerator { private val next = AtomicLong() fun nextId() = next.incrementAndGet() } // lazy instance field: the standard library does the locking class FeeSchedules(loader: () -> Map<String, Long>) { val fees: Map<String, Long> by lazy { loader().toMap() } // SYNCHRONIZED by default }

compare.note: A Kotlin object compiles to the same thing as a Java holder: a class with a static INSTANCE set in its static initializer, so the JVM's class-init lock guarantees one instance. by lazy replaces the whole DCL block (the volatile field, the lock object and the re-check), and it retries on the next access if the initializer throws. So Kotlin makes hand-written singletons and hand-written DCL unnecessary. It does not fix the design problem: a global object that does I/O is as hard to test as a Java static singleton, and the answer in both languages is to inject it.

worked.title: Turn a static singleton into an injected bean, then make its lazy load safe

steps.say: A fee service reads merchant fee schedules through a global singleton. Before reading on, find what stops you from unit-testing feeMinor.
steps.code: class FeeService { long feeMinor(String merchantId, long amountMinor) { long bps = FeeSchedules.getInstance().bpsFor(merchantId); // global; loads from Oracle return amountMinor * bps / 10_000; } }

alt.html: class FeeService { fun feeMinor(merchantId: String, amountMinor: Long): Long { val bps = FeeSchedules.bpsFor(merchantId) // an object: global; loads from Oracle return amountMinor * bps / 10_000 } }

steps.say: The dependency is hidden and global. A test can't pass a fixed schedule, and anything the singleton caches leaks into the next test. Make the dependency visible: an interface, passed through the constructor. Now the test is one line.
steps.code: interface FeeSchedules { long bpsFor(String merchantId); } class FeeService { private final FeeSchedules schedules; // 1. the dependency is in the signature FeeService(FeeSchedules schedules) { this.schedules = schedules; } long feeMinor(String merchantId, long amountMinor) { return amountMinor * schedules.bpsFor(merchantId) / 10_000; } } // test: new FeeService(id -> 290).feeMinor("m-1", 10_000) == 290

alt.html: fun interface FeeSchedules { fun bpsFor(merchantId: String): Long } class FeeService(private val schedules: FeeSchedules) { // 1. the dependency is in the signature fun feeMinor(merchantId: String, amountMinor: Long): Long = amountMinor * schedules.bpsFor(merchantId) / 10_000 } // test: FeeService { 290 }.feeMinor("m-1", 10_000) == 290L

steps.say: Production still wants one schedule table, loaded on first use. The container makes one bean. Inside it the table is an instance field, so the holder idiom can't help: Java uses DCL. Why must the field be volatile? Answer before you read the comment on it. The Kotlin bean is four lines, because by lazy is the DCL block.
steps.code: @ApplicationScoped class OracleFeeSchedules implements FeeSchedules { private final Object lock = new Object(); private volatile Map<String, Long> table; // 2. volatile: readers see the whole map public long bpsFor(String merchantId) { Map<String, Long> t = table; // 3. fast path: one read, no lock if (t == null) { synchronized (lock) { t = table; // 4. re-check under the lock if (t == null) table = t = loadFromOracle(); } } return t.getOrDefault(merchantId, 290L); } private Map<String, Long> loadFromOracle() { return Map.of("m-1", 250L); // SELECT merchant_id, bps FROM fee_schedule } }

alt.html: @ApplicationScoped class OracleFeeSchedules(private val db: FeeDb) : FeeSchedules { // 2-4. by lazy (SYNCHRONIZED) is the volatile field, the lock and the re-check in one line private val table: Map<String, Long> by lazy { db.loadSchedules() } override fun bpsFor(merchantId: String) = table[merchantId] ?: 290L }

lab.title: A lazy registry that loads once, and a harness that proves it
steps: Run the tests. Seven of ten fail: the harness is a stub, and the registry runs its slow loader eight times when eight threads do the first lookup together.

Write Contention.distinctInstances. Start the threads behind two latches (ready and go, as in Race conditions: why count++ lies), store each result in its own array slot, join every thread, then count the results in a set that compares with ==.
Fix CardNetworkRegistry.table() with double-checked locking: a volatile field, a private lock object, and a re-check inside synchronized. Keep the Map.copyOf around the loader's result.
Run the tests until all ten pass, then twice more.
hints: Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>()) is a Set that compares with ==. A HashSet would count eight empty lists as one.
Read the volatile field into a local once at the top and return the local. The fast path then costs one volatile read.
If the loader throws inside the synchronized block, the field is still null and the next caller tries again. You get that for free as long as you assign the field only after loader.get() returns.
lab.done: All ten tests in SingletonTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: The holder idiom and DCL from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In the language you use most, write (a) a lazy singleton FxRates with the holder idiom, and (b) a lazy field fees: Map<String, Long> loaded by loadFees() with double-checked locking, by hand. Then compare with the answer, and read the other language's version too. Did you remember volatile (or @Volatile) and the second null check?

answer.html: // (a) holder idiom: lazy, thread-safe, no lock on the fast path final class FxRates { private FxRates() { } private static final class Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); } static FxRates getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } // (b) double-checked locking for an instance field private final Object lock = new Object(); private volatile Map<String, Long> fees; Map<String, Long> fees() { Map<String, Long> f = fees; // one volatile read if (f == null) { synchronized (lock) { f = fees; // second check, under the lock if (f == null) fees = f = loadFees(); } } return f; }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: // (a) Kotlin's holder: a private object nested in the companion (or just make FxRates an object) class FxRates private constructor() { companion object { private object Holder { val INSTANCE = FxRates() } fun getInstance(): FxRates = Holder.INSTANCE } } // (b) double-checked locking by hand, for practice private val lock = Any() @Volatile private var fees: Map<String, Long>? = null fun fees(): Map<String, Long> { fees?.let { return it } // one volatile read synchronized(lock) { fees?.let { return it } // second check, under the lock return loadFees().also { fees = it } } } // in real Kotlin code, all of (b) is: val fees: Map<String, Long> by lazy { loadFees() }

recap: A design pattern is a name for a recurring design and its trade-offs. Use the names as vocabulary, not as class templates.

Lambdas, sealed types, records and Kotlin delegation turned Strategy, Command, Template Method, State, Visitor, Builder and Decorator into a few lines. Proxy, Chain of Responsibility and Observer moved into frameworks.
Java singletons: an enum when eager is fine, the holder idiom for a lazy static, double-checked locking with volatile for a lazy instance field.
Kotlin object is a thread-safe singleton created on first access. by lazy defaults to SYNCHRONIZED; PUBLICATION may run the initializer once per racing thread.
Prefer a container-managed instance (@ApplicationScoped, a Spring bean) injected through the constructor. A static getInstance() hides the dependency and leaks state between tests.
Prove "only one" with contention: threads released together, a slow constructor, and a count by identity.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to add public static FraudRules getInstance() with a lazy if (instance == null) check to a Quarkus service. Explain what you'd suggest instead, and why.
explain.answer: The plain null check is a check-then-act race: two request threads can both see null and both load the rules. Even a correct lazy singleton makes the dependency hidden and global, so tests can't pass their own rules, and state leaks from one test to the next. I'd make FraudRules an @ApplicationScoped bean and inject it through the constructor; the container builds one instance. If the rules should load lazily inside the bean, that's an instance field, so I'd use double-checked locking with a volatile field, or by lazy in Kotlin, and keep the loader injectable so a test can count how often it runs.

deeper.html:
The JDK is getting its own lazy constant, slowly. JDK 25 shipped StableValue as a preview API (JEP 502). JDK 26 renamed it LazyConstant (JEP 526, second preview), and JDK 27 still has it in preview (JEP 531). LazyConstant.of(() -> load()) promises that when several threads race, only one runs the computation. It can't hold null, and a failed computation is remembered: later calls throw without running it again. That is the opposite of Kotlin's lazy, which retries. Because it is a preview API that has already changed its name once, it stays out of this course's labs. If you want to try it, you need the matching JDK and --enable-preview.

Serialization can break a class-based singleton. Deserializing a Serializable singleton creates a new object unless the class defines readResolve() to return the existing instance. The JVM handles enums specially, which is one reason Effective Java prefers them.

Kotlin's data object gives a singleton a readable toString() and value-style equals. The Kotlin docs warn that serialization or reflection can still produce a second instance, so compare data objects with ==, never with ===. You'll use data object for states that carry no data, such as Pending in a payment state machine, in State and Chain of Responsibility (lesson 9 of this track).
